title: How to write really good Flutter code

segments.text: [MUSIC PLAYING]
MARIAM HASNANY: Hi.
I'm Mariam, a Product Manager for Flutter.
Today, we're going to share seven tools and techniques you
can use right now to make your Flutter code more readable,
scalable, and testable.
I'm joined by Eric and John, who will help me demonstrate
these techniques to build a checkout experience in our Dash
shop app, an exclusive online store for Dash gear-- stuffies,
keyboards, you name it.
ERIC WINDMILL: These techniques will help you build your Flutter
app with a scalable and maintainable app architecture
so it can go the distance.
JOHN RYAN: And we'll also share some tools
that you can use to add features to your app and some cool ways
that AI can use them to Assist you.
[MUSIC PLAYING]
MARIAM HASNANY: All right, let's dive into the code.
The first technique is all about building
a great UI, design using constraints and not fixed sizes.
Flutter makes it possible for us to have the Dash
store available on any device and any screen
with a single code base.
But with ease comes responsibility,
as a wise bird once told me.
It's our job as developers to ensure
the UI is visually responsive while keeping the code readable
and error free.
Designing using constraints makes your widgets
flexible and more reasonable than if they
were using fixed sizes.
That way, you can easily reuse them for mobile, desktop,
or the web.
Essentially, that boils down to three steps-- abstract, measure,
and branch.
ERIC WINDMILL: The UI currently uses Flutter's flex layout
with widgets like row, column, and flex
to help make sure the widgets resize based
on the size of the constraints.
But when the screen gets too small to display everything
or so large that there's wasted screen space,
you need to swap out the layout with an entirely different one
appropriate for the screen size.
So the first step is to identify the UI widgets that
need to change and abstract the underlying data they share.
In this case, the card screen layout
needs to change based on the screen size.
We'll pass the data it needs to render in
via the constructor parameter.
The widget shouldn't care about where the data comes from, just
that it needs to display it.
Next, let's measure the size of your display area.
Use MediaQuery.sizeOf for the entire app window
or LayoutBuilder for the localized constraints.
Since this is a smaller widget that we want to reuse,
we'll use LayoutBuilder.
Finally, we can read the incoming constraints
that LayoutBuilder gives us and return different widgets
based on the available size.
To learn more, check out the layout docs
linked in the description.
MARIAM HASNANY: If our UI layout is broken, or the app freezes,
we could fiddle with the height of the container,
hot reload, fiddle with the height again, hot reload again.
Or we could save some time and skip all of the guesswork
by using DevTools to provide visibility
into the app, such as the exact constraints that the parent
widget is enforcing.
Our second technique is use DevTools.
Keeping accessibility in mind, let's make
the images and the text in the checkout cart
bigger so that they are more visible.
JOHN RYAN: Let's see.
That should be pretty easy.
I'll open up Antigravity and enter a prompt
with the widget I want to change.
OK, so Antigravity made the change.
Now I'll tell it to reload.
And we hit a classic issue, the dreaded layout overflow error.
To help us understand what's going on,
let's use DevTools to see which widget is causing the error.
The Flutter DevTools Inspector highlights these errors
so we can see which widget is causing the issue--
this row widget, which is overflowing.
We can dig into the details ourselves,
or we can use the Dart and Flutter MCP server
to help us fix the issue.
The MCP server makes Flutter's developer tools
available to AI assistants.
To install it in Antigravity, we'll open up the agent panel
and select MCP servers under the additional options dropdown
menu and search for Dart.
Once installed, Antigravity displays the available tools.
When we run our app, our agent can connect to it directly.
And once it's connected, the agent
can read the layout error message using the Get Runtime
Errors tool.
Layout errors contain a lot of details
that Gemini is really good at understanding.
The agent knows how to use the hot reload
and Get Widget Tree Tools to help make sure
that it fixed the layout error.
MARIAM HASNANY: Mixing business logic and UI within a widget
creates massive, unreadable, deeply nested build methods.
By separating your business logic from your UI,
your widgets become easier to reuse, modify, and test.
So technique 3 is building reusable widgets.
ERIC WINDMILL: As mentioned before,
a widget should receive all the configuration it
needs to render as arguments.
It shouldn't have to modify or format any data.
It's only jobs are to render data and listen for user events.
As a rule of thumb, if your widget
is importing low-level libraries,
making remote requests, or interacting with the database,
it's probably not reusable.
In the Dash store app, when a user presses Purchase,
the widget doesn't turn around and call the payments API
directly.
So in order to keep the widget reusable
and only focused on displaying the UI,
that logic is deferred to a different object using
a callback that is passed in as a parameter
to the widget's constructor.
When your widgets are reusable, you
can leverage tools like widget previews.
Widget previews is a developer tool
that complements hot reload, enabling you to experiment
with UI variations in states without running
the full application.
Rather than running an app, navigating to a specific screen,
and getting the app into a specific state
just to test button styles, I can write some widget previews
for that button and pass them in,
enabling me to quickly iterate on designs.
This is straightforward, since our widgets were
built to be reusable, and if you're
building with AI assistance, the Flutter team
has published a skill, Flutter ad widget previews,
that gives instructions to your coding
agents on how to build previews for your app's widget catalog.
JOHN RYAN: This skill is published
as part of Flutter's official skills repository on GitHub,
and it provides instructions for agents
that can be shared and repeated to reliably complete
a task for you.
We authored this skill by grounding it
in our official documentation.
This means that the skills are up to date
and keeps our official docs as the source of truth.
Each skill has a name and description
that tell the agent what it should be used for
and when to use it.
The agent reads it in only when it's
relevant to what you're trying to do.
You can find skills published by the Dart and Flutter
team on GitHub, so you can start using them for your own projects
today.
MARIAM HASNANY: But we didn't just write the skill
and call it a day.
We've rigorously validated it with our evals framework
to ensure it consistently works across use cases.
Our goal is to consistently deliver
tools to developers that help you build better apps.
And with AI's rapid innovation, we
want to make sure that each skill, MCP tool, and model
change is making your apps better.
So we're looking for ways to be more data-driven.
In fact, we're experimenting with evals in public so the code
is open source, and you can check it out
at github.com/flutter/evals.
JOHN RYAN: So now you can see that we have a widget
preview for our widget.
Previews let you test widgets in their various states
and see how they look when placed next to each other.
And we can use our skill to create previews for all
of our important widgets.
So our widgets are looking good.
But now we want to start using them in our app,
and for that, we need to talk about app architecture.
[MUSIC PLAYING]
MARIAM HASNANY: Separation of concerns
is one of the core fundamentals of software development.
In app development, this generally
manifests as a layered architecture.
So the fourth technique is to bake a layer cake.
We layer our apps using MVVM architecture.
All MV-something patterns have a similar layered architecture
using three objects that are roughly equivalent from pattern
to pattern-- a UI layer, a logic layer, and a data layer.
In MVVM, your UI is separated into views,
which are your widgets, and your logic is in the viewmodels.
Viewmodels act as a gatekeeper between the UI and the data
layer.
This separation of logic and UI makes your code
testable and more readable.
ERIC WINDMILL: Viewmodels have three jobs--
transforming app data into data that's ready to be rendered,
telling the data layer when user interaction requires
app data to be modified, and telling the UI when to rebuild.
And for that, we use change notifier.
In the Dash store app, the cart viewmodel provides configuration
for the cart screen and has properties like cart items
and subtotal and methods called add to cart and on purchase.
On purchase is the callback referenced earlier
that we pass into the widget.
When a user presses the Purchase button,
the viewmodel handles the local state, things like toggling,
is loading, and calling notify listeners.
But it defers the data mutation logic
to another layer of the proverbial cake, the data layer.
MARIAM HASNANY: Which brings us to our next technique,
using the repository pattern.
The repository pattern centralizes and abstracts
data access logic.
And it does so using objects called repositories.
A repository manages the data in the data layer.
It's the interface between your app
and external data like server, database, or plugin.
Specifically, in our case, it exposes raw data
from services to the viewmodel.
ERIC WINDMILL: This pattern is used
to establish a single source of truth per data source
in your app and should be the only object that
can fetch from or write data to an external source.
When application data logic is isolated in this way,
it makes your entire code base easier to test and scale.
If you want to try out these architecture
techniques in your own apps, use the official architecture skill
published by the Flutter team to make your AI agent an expert.
MARIAM HASNANY: The sixth technique
is to design for all platforms.
What happens to your data layer when
you need to use native features, like payments?
Flutter uses Dart, but platforms like Android and iOS
expose these features using Kotlin and Swift APIs.
Thankfully, Flutter enables developers
to leverage native device features and third-party APIs
through its massive ecosystem of plugins and packages on pub.dev.
The huge win for developers is that plugins
enable us to write Dart code that works consistently
across all platforms.
And the implementation details are abstracted away
as a package on pub.dev.
JOHN RYAN: Traditionally, to find the right plugin
for payments, I'd leave my IDE, open a browser,
hunt down the right package on pub.dev,
and read through the documentation.
But did you know that your coding agent
can help you with that, too?
Let me show you.
I've got my Dart and Flutter MCP server ready.
So let's ask something, "Help me implement a checkout experience
that uses Apple Pay and Google Pay."
The agent identifies the official pay package.
And as you can see here, it's using the MCP server
to securely interact with external data sources.
In this case, the MCP server enables our agent
to search pub.dev in real time, fetch the latest package
documentation, and analyze the current workspace.
This makes a big difference because including
more context helps the agent write correct code.
If we look at the results, the agent also wrote in the code
to support Apple Pay and Google Pay in our checkout experience.
Of course, if we don't what the agent chose for us,
we can reject the change and provide it with more context.
Because the MCP server searched the package docs,
the code correctly uses the latest API version
rather than relying on training data.
Here's what the checkout experience
looks like on Android and iOS.
MARIAM HASNANY: The new checkout experience is working great.
But now we need to make sure it keeps working reliably.
It's a good idea to add automated tests so we
can know when something breaks.
No matter how much we don't want to do it,
our seventh technique is to write tests.
JOHN RYAN: We've already eaten our vegetables
and designed our app using good architecture patterns,
so it's going to be much easier to add tests.
First, let's add a unit test.
Unit tests can validate the behavior of Dart code
very quickly in parallel.
They're great for testing individual classes or functions
with different inputs to make sure they work correctly
in isolation.
Let's take a look at the cart viewmodel
to see how we can write a test for it.
I can see that it takes a dependency as a parameter,
so we'll want to mock that.
And we'll use the new checks package like this.
You might currently be using the matcher package
to write test expectations like equals or is greater than.
With the checks package, everything is strongly typed,
so your IDE knows which checks are valid for the data
type you're testing.
We also have an agent skill to help
you migrate from the matcher package to the checks package.
Widget tests are great for testing--
you guessed it-- Flutter widgets.
They also run quickly because they
run without a physical device or an emulator
and can tap on widgets, verify the text that's on screen,
and a lot more.
Here's what the widget test for our button looks like.
We can verify that it shows the correct values when we tap.
Finally, let's use an integration test
to verify that this feature works correctly
on a physical device.
Integration tests actually use the same API as widget tests,
so you don't have to learn a new testing framework.
And thanks to our MCP server, our coding agent
can help with this too.
Let me show you how that works.
We've created this Flutter integration testing skill
to help write integration tests.
First, it enables Flutter Driver,
which enables the agent to interact with our app.
From there, it runs the app and interacts with it
to go through the user journey that we're
testing on a real device.
Finally, it captures those steps into an integration test
that we can reliably run.
Now, our integration tests can be
maintained alongside the rest of our test suite.
[MUSIC PLAYING]
MARIAM HASNANY: So let's recap.
We covered seven techniques for writing really good Flutter
code--
designed for constraints, not fixed sizes,
debug using DevTools, build reusable widgets,
bake a layer cake, use a repository pattern,
design for all platforms, and write good tests.
Whether you're writing out code by hand
or iterating with your coding agent,
we hope this helps you write Flutter code that
is more readable, scalable, testable, and faster than ever.
To learn more about Flutter's best practices
and all of our developer tools, point your browser
to flutter.dev.
[MUSIC PLAYING]
